::: {.callout-note title="Summary"}
- I tested whether language models give more in a public goods game when
  giving earns them more tokens.
- In most of the nine setups I tested, giving barely changed. Several of these
  models still answered correctly when I asked them directly which choice
  earns more.
- Two setups gave most of their tokens when giving paid: Claude Sonnet 5.5,
  and GPT-6 Luna with its reasoning setting switched on.
- These are early results from one game. They suggest that a contribution rate
  alone does not tell us why a model gives. They do not show whether a model
  "really" cooperates.
:::

## Background

This project started from a different question. Piedrahita et al. (2025)
found that reasoning models contribute less than other models in public goods
games. I wanted to test this inside one model: train it to reason better, and
measure its cooperation along the way.

I trained Qwen2.5 1.5B and 3B on math problems with reinforcement learning
(GRPO; Shao et al., 2024). On 500 test problems, I did not find a clear
improvement in math accuracy. The 1.5B went from 75.8% to 78.4% (95% CI of the
difference: −0.9 to +6.1 points), and the 3B stayed at 85.6%. The models
mainly learned the answer format that the reward checked (@fig-training). An early bug in my
scoring, which counted only answers in that format, had first made the
training look like a large gain.

![Math accuracy (solid lines) stays flat during training, while the share of
answers written in the `#### <number>` format (dotted lines) rises to almost
100%.](training.png){#fig-training}

So these checkpoints could not support the comparison I had planned. Therefore, I investigated another question: when a model gives tokens in
this game, does its giving depend on the payoff?

## The game

Four players each receive 10 tokens per round, for ten rounds. Each player
decides how many tokens to put into a shared pot. The pot is multiplied and
split equally among the four players.

- **×2 game.** If you put in 10 tokens, the pot grows by 20 and you get 5
  back. You lose 5 tokens, and the group gains. This is the usual dilemma.
- **×6 game.** If you put in 10 tokens, the pot grows by 60 and you get 15
  back. You gain 5 tokens, no matter what the others do.

In the ×6 game, putting in everything gives you the most tokens. A model whose
choices follow its own payoff should give much more there compared to the ×2 game.
I found this test in economics literature. They use this kind of check with people to separate cooperation from
confusion about the rules (Andreoni, 1995; Burton-Chellew et al., 2016).

The model played as one player. The other three players were scripted players who
always give 0 ("free-riders"), so the ×2 and ×6 games differ only in the
multiplier. In other ×2 games I tested multiple setups containing different combinations of these co-players:

- a player who never contributes ("free-riders")

- a player who always gives 10 ("cooperators")

- a player who copies the model's last move ("reciprocators")

- the model itself ("self-play")

I compared two things:

1. **Playing:** how much more of its tokens the model gives in the ×6 game
   than in the ×2 game.
2. **Asking:** outside the game, with the same rules, I asked questions such
   as "If the others put in 0, which leaves you with more tokens: putting in 0
   or putting in 10?" I measured how much more often the model answers "10"
   at ×6 than at ×2.

Each condition had 60 games, 20 for each of three wordings of the rules. I
tested Qwen2.5-Instruct from 1.5B to 32B, Llama 3.3 70B, Claude Sonnet 5.5
with extended thinking off, and GPT-6 Luna with its reasoning setting off and
on.

## Results

### Asking and playing give different pictures

![For each setup, the difference between ×6 and ×2 when asked (horizontal)
and when playing (vertical).](asking-vs-playing.png){#fig-asking
fig-alt="Scatter plot. Qwen 7B, 14B and 32B, Llama 3.3 70B and GPT-6 Luna sit
near zero on the vertical axis, with horizontal values from 0.34 to 0.83.
Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna with reasoning sit at 1.0 horizontally and
about 0.84 vertically. An arrow connects GPT-6 Luna without and with
reasoning."}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Numbers for each setup"}
| Setup | Asking: picks 10 more often at ×6 | Playing: gives more at ×6 | Share given at ×6 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen 1.5B | not scored | −0.00 | 0.32 |
| Qwen 3B | +0.04 | +0.07 | 0.64 |
| Qwen 7B | +0.34 | +0.04 | 0.83 |
| Qwen 14B | +0.57 | +0.05 | 0.42 |
| Qwen 32B | +0.81 | +0.02 | 0.12 |
| Llama 3.3 70B | +0.74 | +0.10 | 0.20 |
| GPT-6 Luna, reasoning off | +0.83 | +0.12 | 0.18 |
| GPT-6 Luna, reasoning on | +1.00 | +0.83 | 0.89 |
| Claude Sonnet 5.5 | +1.00 | +0.85 | 0.94 |

: Differences are ×6 minus ×2, against free-riders. "Share given" is the average share of the 10 tokens over all rounds. The Qwen 1.5B gave too many unreadable answers to score. {#tbl-main}
:::

Qwen 32B, Llama 3.3 70B and Luna with reasoning off mostly answer the payoff
questions correctly (@fig-asking). When they play, they give only 0.02 to 0.12
more at ×6. They contributed only 12% to 20% of their tokens in a game where giving everything
earns the most. For example, when Qwen 32B is asked about the exact situation
of the ×6 game, it answers "put in 10" 73% of the time. In that situation
during play, it gives 7% of its tokens. Some of its written answers do the
arithmetic and then misread it: "my net earnings will be 15 tokens, which is
less than the 10 tokens I started with."

Qwen 7B gives a lot in both games (0.79 at ×2, 0.83 at ×6). So a high share at
×6 alone does not show that a model reacts to the payoff of each strategy.

Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Luna with reasoning on give most of their tokens at ×6.
Their difference between ×6 and ×2 is at least +0.77 under each of the three
wordings.

I noticed the gap between asking and playing in the Qwen models after looking
at their results. Before running Llama and Luna, I wrote the prediction in my
own log, and the gap appeared in both. Similar gaps
have been reported in other decision tasks (Schmied et al., 2025).

### Round by round, there are two patterns

![Share of tokens given in each round against free-riders, in the ×2 game
(blue) and the ×6 game (orange).](rounds.png){#fig-rounds fig-alt="Six small
line charts, one per model, over rounds 1 to 10. Qwen 7B gives about 0.8 in
both games. Qwen 32B and Llama 3.3 70B start near 0.55 in both games and fall
close to zero. GPT-6 Luna starts at 0.86 in the x6 game and 0.58 in the x2
game, then falls to near zero in both. GPT-6 Luna with reasoning and Claude
Sonnet 5.5 stay near 0.9 in the x6 game and fall to zero in the x2 game."}

@fig-rounds shows contributions in each round. The first round is interesting because the
model has not yet seen the others play.
A difference between ×2 and ×6 in round 1 is a reaction to the multiplier
alone. I made this comparison after the main runs.

- **Qwen 32B and Llama 3.3 70B** give about the same in round 1 of both games
  (differences of +0.04 and +0.01, with 95% confidence intervals that include
  zero). They do not react to the multiplier even before any history.
- **Luna with reasoning off** does react at first. In round 1 it gives 0.86 at
  ×6 and 0.58 at ×2 (difference +0.28, 95% CI +0.18 to +0.37). After it sees
  the others give nothing, its giving at ×6 falls to 0.02 in round 2 and stays
  low.
- **Luna with reasoning on** also drops in round 2 (0.67), but returns to
  about 0.9. **Sonnet** stays between 0.88 and 1.00 in every round.

So "does not use the payoff" describes Qwen 32B and Llama better than Luna
without reasoning, which reads the payoff but stops giving after the others
free-ride. I do not yet know why.

### Switching reasoning on

GPT-6 Luna lets the user switch its reasoning setting on and off, with the
same prompts.

![GPT-6 Luna with reasoning off (blue) and on (orange): share of tokens given
in each game. Lines are 95% confidence intervals.](luna-reasoning.png){#fig-luna
fig-alt="Dot plot of six games. With reasoning on, Luna gives less in
self-play, next to cooperators and in the mixed group, about the same next to
reciprocators and free-riders, and much more in the x6 game (0.89 versus
0.18)."}

With reasoning on, its difference between ×6 and ×2 rises from +0.12 to +0.83
(change +0.71, 95% CI +0.67 to +0.74). In the ×2 games (@fig-luna), where
giving costs the player, it gives less with reasoning on: for example, 0.21
less next to players who always give 10. I did not plan this comparison before the runs. I noticed it in a small trial run. It also depends on the wording: the drop next to cooperators is between 0.06 and 0.43, and in self-play, under one of the three wordings, Luna gives slightly more with reasoning on. So I trust only the general direction of this change, not its magnitude.

Piedrahita et al. (2025) and Li and Shirado (2025) found that reasoning
lowers cooperation in economic games. In Luna, reasoning also lowers giving
where giving is costly, but raises it where giving is beneficial. One possible reading
is that reasoning makes Luna's choices follow its own payoff more closely.
This comes from one model, and switching the setting changes more than one
thing (for example, the length limit of the answer), so it is a hypothesis,
not a conclusion.

## What I take from this

- A contribution rate alone does not separate payoff-aware cooperation from
  other patterns, such as following the co-players or giving a fixed amount. A
  version of the game where giving is beneficial (the ×6 game) can be helpful as an extra check.
- Passing this check shows that contributing follows the payoff. It does not show
  the motive behind it. Failing it does not show that a model cannot
  cooperate.
- My pass rules needed work. My first rule (difference above zero with 95%
  confidence) was passed by Qwen 7B, 14B and 32B with differences of only
  +0.02 to +0.05. My stricter rule (a difference of at least +0.30, and at
  least 0.80 given at ×6) cannot be passed by a model that already gives a lot
  at ×2, such as Qwen 7B. Reporting the two numbers separately is clearer.
- Results depend on the wording. Llama's difference is +0.28 in one wording
  and about zero in the other two.

## Current limitations

- The game prompt does not tell the model what goal to pursue. At ×6 against
  free-riders, giving 10 leaves the model with 15 tokens and each free-rider
  with 25. A model that does not want to subsidize free-riders could
  understand the payoff and still give 0. The asking questions, in contrast,
  ask explicitly what earns more.
- Not finding a clear gain in math accuracy does not show that the models'
  reasoning did not change during training.
- Only one model was tested with reasoning on and off.
- Sampling settings and answer length limits differ between some models.
- One simple game, three wordings, and scripted co-players.

## Next steps

Next, I plan to:

- add a version of the prompt that states the goal ("earn as many tokens as
  you can"), to test the free-rider explanation above;
- compare play after the same histories, with and without a short reminder of
  the payoff;
- repeat the reasoning on/off comparison on another model.

I plan to write these results up as a longer report. I am cleaning up the code
and will link the public repository here.
